doc.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: Sitting in with Lionel Hampton and touring Argentina and Europe
summary: He sat in at the Metropole Lounge, was hired on the spot, flew to Buenos Aires, stayed a year, grew tired of few solos, and toured Europe jamming in hot clubs.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: So you start to get established, and what was the Lionel Hampton gig like for you?

Very interesting. What happened, I got to New York and as I was telling a couple of students today, they wanted to know how did I motivate myself and get ahead. I said go to all the jam sessions. Even if it’s not a jam session, if you go to hear somebody play and you feel you’re sure you can play, try to do that. So Lionel Hampton was working at a place called the Metropole Lounge, on Seventh Avenue around 47, 48th street. And he wasn’t using a piano player. You know he was using guitar. Bill Maker was playing guitar

So one of my dearest friends from Chicago named John Neeley, rest his soul, he said why don’t you come by and sit in with Gates we called him. Lionel Hampton called him, “Hey Gates, come on Gates.” You know. So I went by and he introduced me to — and the Metropole was like a long bar, it was long and the band was spread out. You know it wasn’t too wide, just long. So John Neeley introduced me and said, “Hey this is Harold Mabern, he’s from Chicago, can he sit in?” And he said, “Yeah, Gates, you want to play something?” So I got up there, and naturally I knew “Flying Home” from the get go. And because I had been reading music in the big band in Chicago, my eyes were kind of up. And Hamp’s music wasn’t that extreme, it was mostly chords, not a lot of notes, maybe a little passage here. So I sat in and he said, “Yeah, Gates, yeah Gates, I like you” he said, “yeah, Gates, you want to go to Argentina with me?” I said yeah, you know, I didn’t even know if I had a passport then. So he said, “Okay Gates, you’ve got to come down here Thursday and the doctor will be here to give you vaccinations, you know, and you go down and get your passport. During that time you could go to the passport office at Rockefeller Center, you know, like 49th and what was it, Fifth Avenue. So I got my passport. Now one of Hamp’s agents, he was booked by Joe Glaser. And the tickets were already bought for the plane flight. So I think, some kind of way, I took somebody else’s seat. I don’t know who, you know. He said, “Yeah Gates.” So I got there, got my

vaccinations on that Thursday, that Friday I was on my way to Buenos Aires Argentina, and that’s how that happened. So I stayed with the band for a whole year, because, like I said, but at some point I was getting a little tired because I wanted to really play, that’s why I was in New York. I said a big band was one thing but I’m not getting that many solos. Then when I would get a solo, Hamp would come and start playing two fingers at the top so I was really getting a little tired of that. So we did about a six week tour, all through Europe, everywhere. All one nighters, oh man, all one nighters. You know. And what we when we would do a gig, even over there, we would find a place to go jam. They called them hot clubs. And we played tunes like “Straight Street,” John Coltrane’s “Straight Street” and stuff like that. And we would tell Hamp and he’d say, “Hey Gates, you all hanging out tonight?” And we’d say, “Oh no, we’re not hanging out tonight because we’d have Hamp hanging around.” He would get up there and want to play the same songs he’d been playing and come back and do the two piano thing. So when we got back to the States I was living in the Sloan House Y, which was good because I was only paying zero point 75 cents a day. Could you imagine that?
